warmup.q: fun makeCounter(): () -> Int { var count = 0; return { ++count } }. Four threads share one counter and call it 250,000 times each. What does the next call return?
options: It doesn't compile: Kotlin, like Java, won't let a lambda change a captured local
Often less than 1,000,001, and a different number from run to run
Always 250,001, because each thread gets its own copy of count
warmup.why: Kotlin does let a lambda change a captured var. It moves count into a heap object, a Ref$IntRef with one plain int field, that all four threads share. ++count is a read, an add and a write on that field, so increments get lost when two threads read the same old value. Java would refuse to compile the same code; Kotlin compiles it and races.

sections.h: A rule can be a value, like a number or a string
sections.html:
Fraud screening usually starts as one method that grows an if per rule.

Java
static String screen(Payment p, Merchant m) {
    if (p.amountCents() > 500_000) return "amount-limit";
    if (!SERVED.contains(p.country())) return "country-not-served";
    if (!p.currency().equals("EUR")) return "currency-not-supported";
    if (m.isMarketplace() && p.amountCents() < 100) return "micro-payment";
    // ...twelve more, some only for some merchants
    return null;
}
Kotlin
fun screen(p: Payment, m: Merchant): String? {
    if (p.amountCents > 500_000) return "amount-limit"
    if (p.country !in SERVED) return "country-not-served"
    if (p.currency != "EUR") return "currency-not-supported"
    if (m.isMarketplace && p.amountCents < 100) return "micro-payment"
    // ...twelve more, some only for some merchants
    return null
}

Every new rule means editing this method. Every merchant-specific rule adds another flag check. You can't test one rule on its own, reorder them, or let a merchant's configuration pick which ones apply, because the rules aren't things you can hold. They are lines of code.

So make each rule a value. In Kotlin a function has a type, written with an arrow: (Payment) -> Rejection? means "a function that takes a Payment and returns a Rejection or null". You can keep such a function in a val, put it in a list, pass it as an argument and return it from another function, the same way you'd handle an Int. That's what people mean by functions as values.

Java
// Java has no function types; it uses an interface with one method
Function<Payment, Rejection> maxAmount =
        p -> p.amountCents() > 500_000 ? new Rejection("amount-limit", p.id()) : null;
List<Function<Payment, Rejection>> standard = List.of(maxAmount, servedCountry, euroOnly);
Rejection r = maxAmount.apply(payment);
Kotlin
typealias Rule = (Payment) -> Rejection?

val maxAmount: Rule = { p -> if (p.amountCents > 500_000) Rejection("amount-limit", p.id) else null }
val standard: List<Rule> = listOf(maxAmount, servedCountry, euroOnly)
val r = maxAmount(payment)

Now the screening code doesn't know any rule. It runs a list: rules.firstNotNullOfOrNull { rule -> rule(p) }. A marketplace merchant gets standard + noMicroPayments. A test checks one rule with one call.

The two languages spell this differently. Java has no function types, so it uses a functional interface, an interface with one abstract method: Function<T, R>, Predicate<T>, Supplier<T>, or one of your own. You call it by its method name, apply or test. Kotlin has real function types, and you call a value of one like a function: maxAmount(payment). On the JVM, Kotlin's (Payment) -> Rejection? is the interface kotlin.jvm.functions.Function1<Payment, Rejection>, and the call goes to its invoke method. The typealias only gives the type a short name. It creates nothing new.

try.title: Add a rule without touching the others
steps: Run RulesAsValues (or RulesAsValuesJava). Predict first: which payment gets a different answer under the marketplace rules?

Add a rule that only one strict merchant uses: val noUsd: Rule = { p -> if (p.currency == "USD") Rejection("no-usd", p.id) else null }, and a list val strictRules = listOf(noUsd) + standardRules. Print the result for pay_4 under strictRules. (Java: a NO_USD field, and Stream.concat(Stream.of(NO_USD), STANDARD.stream()).toList() for the list.)
Note what you didn't touch: firstRejection and every other rule.

code.title: RulesAsValues.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l02.demo data class Payment(val id: String, val amountCents: Long, val currency: String, val country: String) data class Rejection(val rule: String, val paymentId: String) // A rule is a function from a payment to a rejection, or null when the payment passes. typealias Rule = (Payment) -> Rejection? // Each rule is a value: a lambda stored in a val, ready to go into a list. val maxAmount: Rule = { p -> if (p.amountCents > 500_000) Rejection("amount-limit", p.id) else null } val servedCountry: Rule = { p -> if (p.country in setOf("NL", "BE", "DE")) null else Rejection("country-not-served", p.id) } val euroOnly: Rule = { p -> if (p.currency == "EUR") null else Rejection("currency-not-supported", p.id) } val noMicroPayments: Rule = { p -> if (p.amountCents < 100) Rejection("micro-payment", p.id) else null } // Different merchants get different lists. Adding a rule for one merchant changes nothing above. val standardRules: List<Rule> = listOf(maxAmount, servedCountry, euroOnly) val marketplaceRules: List<Rule> = standardRules + noMicroPayments // Run the rules in order and stop at the first rejection. fun firstRejection(p: Payment, rules: List<Rule>): Rejection? = rules.firstNotNullOfOrNull { rule -> rule(p) } fun main() { val payments = listOf( Payment("pay_1", 12_000, "EUR", "NL"), Payment("pay_2", 900_000, "EUR", "DE"), Payment("pay_3", 50, "EUR", "BE"), Payment("pay_4", 4_000, "USD", "US"), ) for (p in payments) { val standard = firstRejection(p, standardRules)?.rule ?: "ok" val marketplace = firstRejection(p, marketplaceRules)?.rule ?: "ok" println("${p.id}: standard=$standard, marketplace=$marketplace") } }

alt.title: RulesAsValuesJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l02.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.function.Function; /** Java twin of RulesAsValues.kt. A rule is a Function<Payment, Rejection> that returns null when the payment passes. */ public class RulesAsValuesJava { record Payment(String id, long amountCents, String currency, String country) {} record Rejection(String rule, String paymentId) {} // Each rule is a value: a lambda stored in a field, ready to go into a list. static final Function<Payment, Rejection> MAX_AMOUNT = p -> p.amountCents() > 500_000 ? new Rejection("amount-limit", p.id()) : null; static final Function<Payment, Rejection> SERVED_COUNTRY = p -> Set.of("NL", "BE", "DE").contains(p.country()) ? null : new Rejection("country-not-served", p.id()); static final Function<Payment, Rejection> EURO_ONLY = p -> p.currency().equals("EUR") ? null : new Rejection("currency-not-supported", p.id()); static final Function<Payment, Rejection> NO_MICRO_PAYMENTS = p -> p.amountCents() < 100 ? new Rejection("micro-payment", p.id()) : null; // Different merchants get different lists. Adding a rule for one merchant changes nothing above. static final List<Function<Payment, Rejection>> STANDARD = List.of(MAX_AMOUNT, SERVED_COUNTRY, EURO_ONLY); static final List<Function<Payment, Rejection>> MARKETPLACE = plus(STANDARD, NO_MICRO_PAYMENTS); static <T> List<T> plus(List<T> list, T extra) { List<T> copy = new ArrayList<>(list); copy.add(extra); return List.copyOf(copy); } // Run the rules in order and stop at the first rejection. A rule is called with apply. static Rejection firstRejection(Payment p, List<Function<Payment, Rejection>> rules) { for (Function<Payment, Rejection> rule : rules) { Rejection r = rule.apply(p); if (r != null) return r; } return null; } static String name(Rejection r) { return r == null ? "ok" : r.rule(); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Payment> payments = List.of( new Payment("pay_1", 12_000, "EUR", "NL"), new Payment("pay_2", 900_000, "EUR", "DE"), new Payment("pay_3", 50, "EUR", "BE"), new Payment("pay_4", 4_000, "USD", "US")); for (Payment p : payments) { System.out.println(p.id() + ": standard=" + name(firstRejection(p, STANDARD)) + ", marketplace=" + name(firstRejection(p, MARKETPLACE))); } } }

try.expect: pay_3 (50 cents) passes the standard rules and is rejected as micro-payment by the marketplace list. Under strictRules, pay_4 is rejected as no-usd instead of country-not-served: the order of the list is the order of evaluation, and the first rejection wins. firstRejection didn't change, because it never knew any rule.

refs.title: Higher-order functions and lambdas: function types (Kotlin docs)

sections.h: Lambdas, references and the other ways to make a function value
sections.html:
A lambda is the most common way to write a function value, but it is one of four. All four below have the same type.

Java
Predicate<Long> lambda = cents -> cents > 500_000;
Predicate<Long> anon = new Predicate<>() {                    // anonymous class
    public boolean test(Long cents) { return cents > 500_000; }
};
Predicate<Long> ref = Limits::isOverLimit;                     // method reference
Predicate<Long> obj = new OverLimit(500_000);                  // class implementing Predicate
Kotlin
val lambda: (Long) -> Boolean = { cents -> cents > 500_000 }
val anon: (Long) -> Boolean = fun(cents: Long): Boolean { return cents > 500_000 }
val ref: (Long) -> Boolean = ::isOverLimit                     // function reference
val obj: (Long) -> Boolean = OverLimit(500_000)                // class OverLimit : (Long) -> Boolean

A lambda with one parameter can leave it unnamed and use it: { it > 500_000 }. Its value is its last expression. That's also why a bare return inside a lambda doesn't compile ('return' is prohibited here.): return belongs to the enclosing fun, not to the lambda. If you want early exits, write an anonymous function, where return means what it means everywhere else, or use a labelled return@label.

A function reference turns a named function into a value. ::isOverLimit points at a top-level function. Payment::isDomestic is unbound: its type takes the receiver as the first parameter, (Payment) -> Boolean. limits::check is bound to one limits object, so its type has only the remaining parameters. ::Rejection points at the constructor.

Two more shapes show up in Kotlin APIs. A function type can be nullable: ((Rejection) -> Unit)? is an optional callback. Mind the parentheses. Without them, (Rejection) -> Unit? is a function that returns Unit?. You call a nullable one with onReject?.invoke(r). And a function type can have a receiver. In Long.() -> Boolean, the lambda body sees the Long as this, so you can write { this % 100 == 0L }. Receivers are how apply and buildList work. Lesson 6 of this track covers the scope functions, and the Advanced Kotlin track has a lesson on type-safe DSLs. Java has neither: a Consumer<Rejection> parameter may simply be null by convention, and there is no receiver.

try.title: Four ways, one type
steps: Open FourWays.kt (or FourWaysJava.java). Predict the four booleans it prints for 12000, 900000 and -5.

In overLimitLambda, add the same early exit the anonymous function has: if (cents < 0) return true on its own line before cents > 500_000. Run it and read the error. Then fix it with a label: write check@{ cents -> ... } and return@check true.

code.title: FourWays.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l02.demo // The same "is this amount over the limit?" check, written four ways. All four have the type (Long) -> Boolean. // 1. A lambda. val overLimitLambda: (Long) -> Boolean = { cents -> cents > 500_000 } // 2. An anonymous function. Same type, but `return` means "return from this function". val overLimitAnon: (Long) -> Boolean = fun(cents: Long): Boolean { if (cents < 0) return true // a negative amount is suspicious too return cents > 500_000 } // 3. A reference to an ordinary function. fun isOverLimit(cents: Long): Boolean = cents > 500_000 val overLimitRef: (Long) -> Boolean = ::isOverLimit // 4. A class that implements the function type. class OverLimit(private val limitCents: Long) : (Long) -> Boolean { override fun invoke(cents: Long): Boolean = cents > limitCents } // A function type with a receiver: inside the lambda, `this` is the Long. val isRound: Long.() -> Boolean = { this % 100 == 0L } // A nullable function type: the caller may pass no callback at all. fun check(cents: Long, rule: (Long) -> Boolean, onHit: ((Long) -> Unit)? = null): Boolean { val hit = rule(cents) if (hit) onHit?.invoke(cents) return hit } fun main() { val rules = listOf(overLimitLambda, overLimitAnon, overLimitRef, OverLimit(500_000)) for (cents in listOf(12_000L, 900_000L, -5L)) println("$cents -> ${rules.map { rule -> rule(cents) }}") println("120000.isRound() = ${120_000L.isRound()}, 120001.isRound() = ${120_001L.isRound()}") check(900_000, overLimitRef) { println("callback: $it is over the limit") } println("no callback given: ${check(900_000, overLimitRef)}") }

alt.title: FourWaysJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l02.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.LongConsumer; import java.util.function.Predicate; /** * Java twin of FourWays.kt. Java has no function types, so each value is an instance of a functional * interface, here Predicate<Long>. Java has no receiver types either: Kotlin's Long.() -> Boolean has no twin. */ public class FourWaysJava { // 1. A lambda. static final Predicate<Long> OVER_LIMIT_LAMBDA = cents -> cents > 500_000; // 2. An anonymous class: the closest Java has to an anonymous function. `return` leaves test(). static final Predicate<Long> OVER_LIMIT_ANON = new Predicate<>() { @Override public boolean test(Long cents) { if (cents < 0) return true; // a negative amount is suspicious too return cents > 500_000; } }; // 3. A method reference to an ordinary method. static boolean isOverLimit(Long cents) { return cents > 500_000; } static final Predicate<Long> OVER_LIMIT_REF = FourWaysJava::isOverLimit; // 4. A class that implements the interface. static final class OverLimit implements Predicate<Long> { private final long limitCents; OverLimit(long limitCents) { this.limitCents = limitCents; } @Override public boolean test(Long cents) { return cents > limitCents; } } // An optional callback: Java can't say "nullable" in the type, so null is just allowed by convention. static boolean check(long cents, Predicate<Long> rule, LongConsumer onHit) { boolean hit = rule.test(cents); if (hit && onHit != null) onHit.accept(cents); return hit; } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Predicate<Long>> rules = List.of(OVER_LIMIT_LAMBDA, OVER_LIMIT_ANON, OVER_LIMIT_REF, new OverLimit(500_000)); for (long cents : new long[] {12_000L, 900_000L, -5L}) { System.out.println(cents + " -> " + rules.stream().map(rule -> rule.test(cents)).toList()); } check(900_000, OVER_LIMIT_REF, c -> System.out.println("callback: " + c + " is over the limit")); System.out.println("no callback given: " + check(900_000, OVER_LIMIT_REF, null)); } }

try.expect: 12000 prints four false, 900000 four true. For -5 only the anonymous function says true, because it is the only one with the early return. The bare return in the lambda fails with 'return' is prohibited here.; the labelled return@check true returns from the lambda and compiles. The Java version has no isRound line, because Java has no receiver types.

sections.h: What a lambda turns into on the JVM
sections.html:
A function value is an object, so something has to create it. What that costs depends on how you wrote it, and Kotlin and Java don't agree on every case.

Since Kotlin 2.0, lambdas compile to invokedynamic by default, the mechanism Java has used for lambdas since Java 8. The compiler moves the lambda body into a private static method, such as nonCapturing$lambda$0. At the place where the lambda is created, it emits an invokedynamic instruction whose bootstrap method is LambdaMetafactory.metafactory. The first time that instruction runs, the JVM spins up a hidden class that implements Function1 and calls the private method. No .class file for the lambda shows up in your build output. (Kotlin 1.x generated one class per lambda, and the compiler flag -Xlambdas=class still brings that back.)

How many objects you get depends on what the lambda captures:

Java
nonCapturing() == nonCapturing();       // true: one shared instance
capturing(30) == capturing(30);         // false: a new object per evaluation
Kotlin
nonCapturing() === nonCapturing()       // true: one shared instance
capturing(30) === capturing(30)         // false: a new object per evaluation
capturing(30) == capturing(30)          // false: lambdas have no equals

A non-capturing lambda uses nothing from outside its body, so one instance serves every call. A capturing lambda holds the values it uses (feeCents here), so each evaluation allocates a new object with those values inside.

Function references are where Kotlin differs from Java. In Kotlin 2.4.21, ::addFee and m::withFee still compile to real classes, LambdaShapesKt$topLevelRef$1 and LambdaShapesKt$boundRef$1, which extend kotlin.jvm.internal.FunctionReferenceImpl. An unbound reference is a singleton held in a static INSTANCE field. A bound one is a new object each time, holding its receiver. Java method references go through invokedynamic like lambdas do, and leave no class file behind.

One more cost hides in the types. (Long) -> Long is Function1<Long, Long>, which is generic, so a call through it boxes the long into a java.lang.Long and back. Java avoids that with primitive interfaces like LongUnaryOperator. Kotlin has no primitive function interfaces. It avoids the box another way, with inline functions, which the next lesson covers.

None of this is a reason to avoid lambdas. A capturing lambda costs one small object per evaluation, which the JVM allocates cheaply. It starts to matter in two places: a capturing lambda created inside a hot loop, and code that compares function values with ==, which never works for lambdas.

try.title: Count the objects and the class files
steps: Run LambdaShapes (or LambdaShapesJava). Before you look, predict the five true or false answers.
From labs/, list the compiled demo classes: ls functional/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/functional/l02/demo/. Look for a class per lambda and a class per reference.
Run javap -c -p functional/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/functional/l02/demo/LambdaShapesKt.class and find the first instruction of nonCapturing and of topLevelRef.

code.title: LambdaShapes.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l02.demo fun addFee(cents: Long): Long = cents + 30 fun nonCapturing(): (Long) -> Long = { it + 30 } // uses nothing from outside fun capturing(feeCents: Long): (Long) -> Long = { it + feeCents } // captures feeCents fun topLevelRef(): (Long) -> Long = ::addFee // a function reference class Merchant(private val feeCents: Long) { fun withFee(cents: Long): Long = cents + feeCents } fun boundRef(m: Merchant): (Long) -> Long = m::withFee // a reference bound to one object fun main() { val m = Merchant(30) println("non-capturing lambda: same object every time? ${nonCapturing() === nonCapturing()}") println("capturing lambda: same object every time? ${capturing(30) === capturing(30)}") println("capturing lambdas equal with == ? ${capturing(30) == capturing(30)}") println("unbound reference ::addFee: same object? ${topLevelRef() === topLevelRef()}") println("bound reference m::withFee: same object? ${boundRef(m) === boundRef(m)}") println() val lambda = nonCapturing().javaClass val ref = topLevelRef().javaClass println("lambda class: ${lambda.name} (hidden: ${lambda.isHidden})") println("reference class: ${ref.name} (hidden: ${ref.isHidden}, extends ${ref.superclass.simpleName})") }

alt.title: LambdaShapesJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l02.demo; import java.util.function.LongUnaryOperator; /** * Java twin of LambdaShapes.kt. In Java both lambdas and method references go through invokedynamic, * so neither leaves a class file behind. Compare the last two lines with the Kotlin version. */ public class LambdaShapesJava { static long addFee(long cents) { return cents + 30; } static LongUnaryOperator nonCapturing() { return c -> c + 30; } // uses nothing from outside static LongUnaryOperator capturing(long feeCents) { return c -> c + feeCents; } // captures feeCents static LongUnaryOperator staticRef() { return LambdaShapesJava::addFee; } // a method reference static final class Shop { private final long feeCents; Shop(long feeCents) { this.feeCents = feeCents; } long withFee(long cents) { return cents + feeCents; } } static LongUnaryOperator boundRef(Shop s) { return s::withFee; } // bound to one object public static void main(String[] args) { Shop s = new Shop(30); System.out.println("non-capturing lambda: same object every time? " + (nonCapturing() == nonCapturing())); System.out.println("capturing lambda: same object every time? " + (capturing(30) == capturing(30))); System.out.println("capturing lambdas equal with equals? " + capturing(30).equals(capturing(30))); System.out.println("static method ref: same object? " + (staticRef() == staticRef())); System.out.println("bound method ref s::withFee: same object? " + (boundRef(s) == boundRef(s))); System.out.println(); Class<?> lambda = nonCapturing().getClass(); Class<?> ref = staticRef().getClass(); System.out.println("lambda class: " + lambda.getName() + " (hidden: " + lambda.isHidden() + ")"); System.out.println("method ref class: " + ref.getName() + " (hidden: " + ref.isHidden() + ")"); } }

The Kotlin lambda's class is a hidden class named like LambdaShapesKt$$Lambda/0x..., while the reference's class is an ordinary class, LambdaShapesKt$topLevelRef$1, that extends FunctionReferenceImpl. The directory has LambdaShapesKt$topLevelRef$1.class and LambdaShapesKt$boundRef$1.class, and no file for any lambda. In the Java version, the lambda and the method reference are both hidden classes. javap shows invokedynamic ... invoke:()Lkotlin/jvm/functions/Function1; in nonCapturing and getstatic ... LambdaShapesKt$topLevelRef$1.INSTANCE in topLevelRef.

refs.title: What's new in Kotlin 2.0.0: lambdas via invokedynamic

sections.h: A closure keeps its variables, and a captured var is a shared box
sections.html:
A lambda can use variables from the function that created it, and it keeps them after that function has returned. Code plus the variables it captured is called a closure.

Java
static IntSupplier makeCounter() {
    int[] count = {0};                  // Java makes you build the box yourself
    return () -> ++count[0];
}
Kotlin
fun makeCounter(): () -> Int {
    var count = 0
    return { ++count }                  // the lambda keeps count alive
}

Call makeCounter() twice and you get two counters, each with its own count. Each one returns 1, 2, 3 and so on.

Look at what the Java version needed. Java refuses to capture a local variable that changes: local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final. The reason is mechanical. A local variable lives in the method's stack frame, and that frame is gone once makeCounter returns. The lambda outlives it, so all it can take is a copy of the value, and copying a variable that keeps changing would be confusing. Java programmers work around it with a one-element array or an AtomicInteger: an object on the heap that both sides point to.

Kotlin builds that object for you, silently. When a lambda captures a var, the compiler moves the variable into a small heap object, kotlin.jvm.internal.Ref$IntRef (or LongRef, ObjectRef and so on), and both the function and the lambda use its field. The field is a plain public int element, with no volatile and no lock.

That's fine on one thread. It's a bug as soon as two threads share the closure. ++count becomes "read element, add one, write element", the same read-modify-write as count++ in the race conditions lesson, and updates get lost. Nothing in the Kotlin source looks shared. The sharing comes from the box the compiler made.

There are two fixes. Share a thread-safe object instead of a var: capture val count = AtomicLong() and call count.incrementAndGet(). Or, better, don't share at all. Let each task count its own work and combine the results at the end with a sum or a fold. The second fix is the functional one, and it keeps working when the tasks move to other machines.

try.title: Lose updates, then fix it two ways
steps: Run CapturedRace (or CapturedRaceJava). Four pool threads each add 1 to a captured total 250,000 times, ten runs in a row.
Fix it by sharing a thread-safe object: make it val total = AtomicLong() (Java: AtomicLong total = new AtomicLong()), call total.incrementAndGet() in the loop, and print total.get(). Run it.

Undo that, and fix it by not sharing: make each task return its own count, pool.submit(Callable { go.await(); var mine = 0L; repeat(250_000) { mine += 1 }; mine }), then add up tasks.sumOf { it.get() }. (Java: return mine from the lambda and add up the Future<Long> results.) Run it.

code.title: CapturedRace.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l02.demo import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.Executors // Four pool threads add to one captured var. The var lives in a Ref.LongRef box with a plain field. fun main() { val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4) repeat(10) { run -> var total = 0L // captured below, so it becomes a Ref.LongRef val go = CountDownLatch(1) // start all four tasks at the same moment val tasks = List(4) { pool.submit { go.await() repeat(250_000) { total += 1 } // read element, add 1, write element } } go.countDown() tasks.forEach { it.get() } println("run %2d: expected 1,000,000, got %,9d (lost %,d)".format(run + 1, total, 1_000_000 - total)) } pool.shutdown() }

alt.title: CapturedRaceJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l02.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** * Java twin of CapturedRace.kt. Java refuses to capture a local that changes: * long total = 0; ... () -> total += 1 * error: local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final * So Java programmers write the box by hand, a one-element array. That is what Kotlin's Ref.LongRef is. */ public class CapturedRaceJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4); for (int run = 1; run <= 10; run++) { long[] total = {0}; // the hand-made box: a plain array slot CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); // start all four tasks at the same moment List<Future<?>> tasks = new ArrayList<>(); for (int t = 0; t < 4; t++) { tasks.add(pool.submit(() -> { go.await(); for (int i = 0; i < 250_000; i++) total[0] += 1; // read, add 1, write return null; })); } go.countDown(); for (Future<?> f : tasks) f.get(); System.out.printf("run %2d: expected 1,000,000, got %,9d (lost %,d)%n", run, total[0], 1_000_000 - total[0]); } pool.shutdown(); } }

try.expect: The broken version loses updates in several of the ten runs, by different amounts each time. One run here printed 669,421 and 453,808, then four correct runs, then 750,000. Both fixes print exactly 1,000,000 every run. The don't-share version has no contention at all: mine is only ever touched by one thread, so the compiler keeps it a plain local (repeat is inline, so no lambda captures it).

refs.title: Ref.java: the boxes for captured vars (Kotlin stdlib source)

analogy: A closure is a pocket calculator you take home from the office with a number still in its memory. The office, the function that made it, has closed for the day, but the number goes where the calculator goes. Two colleagues can each take their own calculator and keep separate totals. The trouble starts when two people share one calculator and both press M+ at the same moment: each reads the memory, adds, and writes back, and one press disappears. The analogy breaks because a real calculator takes one key press at a time. A Ref box has no such protection.
world: Rules as values fit the per-merchant configuration your payment service already has. Build a Map<MerchantTier, List<Rule>> once at startup in an @ApplicationScoped Quarkus bean, look up the list on each authorization, and run it. Kafka consumers are where closures bite. A var processed = 0 captured by the handler lambda of a listener running with concurrency 4 is one Ref box shared by four threads, and your metric undercounts under load. Use a Micrometer counter or a LongAdder for shared counts, and keep per-message state inside the handler. A Temporal activity retried on another worker never sees the closure at all, so don't keep business state in one.
mistake: The common mistake is changing a captured var from a lambda that runs somewhere else: a callback, a CompletableFuture stage, a pool task, a parallel stream. Kotlin compiles it without a word, because capturing a var is legal; the variable just becomes a Ref box with a plain field. Java stops you with the effectively-final error, and then people reach for long[] total = {0}, which is the same box with the same race. Don't accumulate through shared state. Return a value from each task and combine the values (sum, fold). If you really need one live shared count, capture a val that holds an AtomicLong or a LongAdder.

compare.title: Rules and closures with functional interfaces and with function types

java.title: Rules.java
java.html: import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Function; import java.util.function.IntSupplier; record Payment(String id, long amountCents, String country) {} record Rejection(String rule, String paymentId) {} final class Rules { // a function value is an instance of a functional interface static Function<Payment, Rejection> amountAtMost(long limit) { return p -> p.amountCents() > limit ? new Rejection("amount-limit", p.id()) : null; // captures limit } static Rejection firstRejection(Payment p, List<Function<Payment, Rejection>> rules) { return rules.stream() .map(rule -> rule.apply(p)) // called by its method name .filter(r -> r != null) .findFirst() .orElse(null); } // a captured local that changes is a compile error; the array is the box, built by hand static IntSupplier makeCounter() { int[] count = {0}; return () -> ++count[0]; } }

kotlin.title: Rules.kt
kotlin.html: data class Payment(val id: String, val amountCents: Long, val country: String) data class Rejection(val rule: String, val paymentId: String) typealias Rule = (Payment) -> Rejection? // a real function type: Function1 on the JVM fun amountAtMost(limit: Long): Rule = { p -> // captures limit if (p.amountCents > limit) Rejection("amount-limit", p.id) else null } fun firstRejection(p: Payment, rules: List<Rule>): Rejection? = rules.firstNotNullOfOrNull { rule -> rule(p) } // called like a function // capturing a var is allowed; the compiler builds the Ref box for you fun makeCounter(): () -> Int { var count = 0 return { ++count } }

compare.note: Kotlin has function types; Java has functional interfaces. That changes three things you notice every day. Kotlin calls a function value with f(x), where Java needs the interface's method name (apply, test, getAsInt), and Kotlin has one family of types, (A) -> B, where Java has dozens of interfaces, primitive ones included. Kotlin's types can say "may be null" (Rejection?, ((Rejection) -> Unit)?), so a rule that returns null shows it in its type. And Kotlin lets a lambda capture a var by moving it into a Ref box, where Java insists on effectively final locals and makes you write the box. Under the hood both compile lambdas with invokedynamic; only Kotlin's function references still compile to classes.

worked.title: Find the hidden shared box in a settlement job

steps.say: A settlement job posts payments to the ledger in chunks of 500 on a thread pool and adds up what it settled. Under load the total comes out a little low, and only sometimes. Find the shared state before reading on.
steps.code: fun settle(batch: List<Payment>, pool: ExecutorService): Long { var settledCents = 0L val futures = batch.chunked(500).map { chunk -> pool.submit { chunk.forEach { p -> if (ledger.post(p)) settledCents += p.amountCents } } } futures.forEach { it.get() } return settledCents }

alt.html: // The Java version doesn't compile as written: static long settle(List<Payment> batch, ExecutorService pool) throws Exception { long settledCents = 0; List<Future<?>> futures = new ArrayList<>(); for (List<Payment> chunk : chunks(batch, 500)) { futures.add(pool.submit(() -> { for (Payment p : chunk) if (ledger.post(p)) settledCents += p.amountCents(); // error: local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final })); } for (Future<?> f : futures) f.get(); return settledCents; }

steps.say: 1. Find the box. settledCents is a var captured by the lambda passed to submit, which runs on pool threads. The compiler turned it into one Ref$LongRef, and every chunk task does read, add, write on its plain element field. (forEach is inline, so its lambda doesn't count; the submit lambda is the one that captures.) Java refused the same code, and the usual Java workaround is the same box written by hand.
steps.code: // roughly what the compiler made of it val settledCents = Ref.LongRef() // one box on the heap pool.submit { ...; settledCents.element += p.amountCents } // every task, on every thread

alt.html: long[] settledCents = {0}; // the box Java makes you write pool.submit(() -> { ...; settledCents[0] += p.amountCents(); }); // the same race

steps.say: 1. Don't share. Make each task return its own subtotal, and add the subtotals up on the calling thread. Each task's lambda now captures only its chunk, which nobody changes. Self-check: why is sumOf inside the task safe? (It runs on one thread over that task's own chunk, and its running total is a local.)
steps.code: fun settle(batch: List<Payment>, pool: ExecutorService): Long { val futures = batch.chunked(500).map { chunk -> pool.submit(Callable { // 1. each task returns a value chunk.sumOf { p -> if (ledger.post(p)) p.amountCents else 0L } }) } return futures.sumOf { it.get() } // 2. combine on one thread }

alt.html: static long settle(List<Payment> batch, ExecutorService pool) throws Exception { List<Future<Long>> futures = new ArrayList<>(); for (List<Payment> chunk : chunks(batch, 500)) { futures.add(pool.submit(() -> chunk.stream() // 1. each task returns a value .mapToLong(p -> ledger.post(p) ? p.amountCents() : 0L) .sum())); } long total = 0; for (Future<Long> f : futures) total += f.get(); // 2. combine on one thread return total; }

steps.say: 1. If you really need a live shared number, say a progress gauge while the job runs, share a thread-safe object through a val, never a var. LongAdder spreads the contention over several cells and is cheaper than AtomicLong when many threads add at once.
steps.code: val settledSoFar = LongAdder() // a val: the reference never changes pool.submit { chunk.forEach { p -> if (ledger.post(p)) settledSoFar.add(p.amountCents) } }

alt.html: LongAdder settledSoFar = new LongAdder(); // effectively final, so Java is happy too pool.submit(() -> { for (Payment p : chunk) if (ledger.post(p)) settledSoFar.add(p.amountCents()); });

lab.title: Rules as values, and a counter that survives eight threads
steps: Run the tests. All ten fail: nine with NotImplementedError, and the shared-counter test with a short count, something like but was: 1447832L where 1,600,001 was expected.

In Rules.kt, write amountAtMost (return a lambda that captures limitCents), countryServed (a lambda in a val) and supportedCurrency. Then replace the body of currencyRule with the reference ::supportedCurrency.
Write firstRejection and allRejections. firstRejection must stop at the first rejection: one test counts calls to a later rule.
Write screen. The callback is optional, so call it with ?.invoke.
In Counters.kt, write makeCounter. Then fix makeSharedCounter so the 8-thread test passes. Keep the return type () -> Long.
Run the tests until all ten pass, then run them twice more. A race fix has to pass every time.
hints: rules.firstNotNullOfOrNull { rule -> rule(payment) } returns the first non-null result and stops there. mapNotNull keeps every non-null result.
If countryServed gives you a type error, name the lambda's parameter and make both branches of the if produce a Rejection?: { p -> if (p.country in SERVED_COUNTRIES) null else Rejection(...) }.
A val that holds an AtomicLong is safe to capture: the reference never changes, and incrementAndGet() is one atomic step that returns the new value.
lab.done: All ten tests in FunctionValuesTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Write two closures from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write feeRule(percent, minCents), which returns a function from an amount in cents to a fee: amount * percent / 100, but never less than minCents. Then write makeCounter(), and add a one-line comment saying what the compiler does with its captured var. Write both in Kotlin and in Java, and note the one line Java refuses to compile.

answer.html: fun feeRule(percent: Int, minCents: Long): (Long) -> Long = { amountCents -> maxOf(amountCents * percent / 100, minCents) } // captures percent and minCents fun makeCounter(): () -> Int { var count = 0 // captured var: moved into a Ref.IntRef box with a plain int field return { ++count } } // val fee = feeRule(2, 50) // fee(10_000) == 200, fee(1_000) == 50 // val c = makeCounter(); c(); c() == 2

alt.html: static LongUnaryOperator feeRule(int percent, long minCents) { return amountCents -> Math.max(amountCents * percent / 100, minCents); } static IntSupplier makeCounter() { // int count = 0; return () -> ++count; <- won't compile: // local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final int[] count = {0}; // the box, written by hand return () -> ++count[0]; }

recap: A function type such as (Payment) -> Rejection? is a type like any other: store its values, put them in lists, pass them and return them. On the JVM it is Function1.
Java uses functional interfaces (Function, Predicate, your own) and calls them by method name. Kotlin calls a function value like a function.
Lambdas, anonymous functions, references and classes that implement a function type all make function values. A bare return is prohibited in a lambda that isn't inlined.

Kotlin 2.x compiles lambdas with invokedynamic: no class file, one shared instance when nothing is captured, a new object per evaluation when something is. Function references still compile to classes.
A closure keeps the variables it captured. A captured var lives in a Ref box with a plain field, so a closure shared between threads loses updates.
Share a val that holds an atomic or, better, return a value from each task and combine the values.

explain.prompt: A teammate's Kotlin counter, a var n = 0 captured by a lambda that four threads call, loses counts. They say: "There's no shared field anywhere in my code." Explain what the compiler did and what you would change.
explain.answer: A local variable normally lives in the stack frame of the function that declares it, and the lambda outlives that frame. So when a lambda captures a var, Kotlin moves the variable into a small object on the heap, a Ref$IntRef, and both the function and the lambda use its element field. That field is the shared field: all four threads reach it through the same lambda. It's a plain field, so n++ is a read, an add and a write that two threads can interleave, and increments get lost. Java would have refused to compile the capture. I'd stop sharing: have each thread or task count its own work and add the counts up at the end. If a live shared count is really needed, I'd capture a val holding a LongAdder or AtomicLong instead of a var.

deeper.html:
javap -v shows how invokedynamic is wired. Each lambda site has an entry in the class's BootstrapMethods table pointing at LambdaMetafactory.metafactory, with three arguments: the erased method type of invoke, (Ljava/lang/Object;)Ljava/lang/Object;, a handle to the private static method holding the body, and the instantiated type, (Ljava/lang/Long;)Ljava/lang/Long; for a (Long) -> Long. The erased signature is why a call through Function1 boxes: invoke takes and returns Object.

Kotlin 2.0's switch to invokedynamic changed three visible things, according to its release notes. These lambdas aren't serializable, the experimental reflect() API doesn't support them, and toString() prints the hidden class name, something like LambdaShapesKt$$Lambda/0x...@1b6d3586, instead of a readable description of the function type. A test or log that matched on the old text breaks after the upgrade. Annotate a single lambda with @JvmSerializableLambda, or compile the module with -Xlambdas=class, to get the old class-per-lambda behaviour.

SAM conversions went to invokedynamic earlier, in Kotlin 1.5. That covers a Kotlin lambda passed where Java expects a Runnable or Comparator, and a lambda for your own fun interface:

Java
@FunctionalInterface
interface FeeRule { long feeFor(long amountCents); }

FeeRule flat = amountCents -> 30;              // Java lambdas have always worked this way
Runnable task = () -> System.out.println("settled");
Kotlin
fun interface FeeRule { fun feeFor(amountCents: Long): Long }

val flat = FeeRule { 30 }                  // a SAM conversion: invokedynamic, no class file
val task = Runnable { println("settled") } // the same for a Java interface

A fun interface is worth using when a function type needs a name in a public API, or when Java callers will implement it, since Java code can't write a lambda for Function1 as naturally as for an interface named after its job.
